summary:
La Pampa is a province of Argentina and stands under the national framework, which remains among the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated on 24 May 2012, and permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prison.

Trans people hired under the national one-percent Trans Labor Quota have been dismissed, and the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI has been abolished, removing the federal body that handled discrimination complaints.

Activists report that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has worsened since the Milei government took office, and that it is worst outside Buenos Aires, in the more conservative interior provinces. La Pampa lies in that interior, away from the capital.

Violence reached a documented national high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a rise of 62% on 2024 and a ten-year record, averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026.

Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space, and beatings were the main modality. Institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, 32% of 2025 incidents took place in police stations or prisons, and 43% of perpetrators were strangers to their victims.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated-crime aggravator therefore does not apply in the case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed on 4 April 2025 by the Washington Blade, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, who was stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

Legal experts called the February 2025 decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene.

Agencia Presentes described the 2025 hate-crime figures, published on 19 March 2026, as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.
localsOnly:
Residents of La Pampa can change their legal gender under Law 26.743 without surgery, without hormone treatment and without a court order, and that statutory route has not been repealed.

Residents who lost work under the one-percent Trans Labor Quota have no reinstatement recorded in these sources, and the abolition of INADI removes the federal anti-discrimination channel through which such dismissals were previously pursued.

The decree of 5 February 2025 on gender-affirming care applies to minors in the province, and the second decree governs how transgender people are housed in prison, which affects trans detainees held in La Pampa.

Institutional violence is the dominant pattern in the national data: 64 cases in 2025 against 17 in 2024, with roughly a third of all 2025 incidents occurring inside police stations or prisons, and security-force personnel among the most frequent perpetrators.

Provincial anti-discrimination protections exist alongside the national framework, but the province's residents are covered by a national record in which hate crimes rose 62% in a single year to 227 incidents.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation against the February 2025 decree on minors is not recorded in the sources available here, so its binding status in La Pampa is unresolved.

La Pampa has no local reporting infrastructure generating separate hate-crime records, so the province's own incidence cannot be stated; the national figures stand in for it and no province-level breakdown is sourced.

The finding that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers is worst in the interior provinces rests on activist testimony reported in April 2025, not on official statistics, and no province-specific policing data for La Pampa is available.

Whether the abolition of INADI has left any federal or provincial complaint mechanism functioning in the province is not sourced here.
